To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the IL-2 response defect of SLE is not due to an intrinsic defect of IL-2 responsive cells, but rather is due to a reversible defect of precursor frequency and/or kinetics.

(1) SLE peripheral blood T lymphocytes have a reversible defect in IL-2 responsiveness, which is not more frequent in those with active SLE; (2) SLE peripheral T lymphocytes have an abnormality in the kinetics of their IL-2 response that is not found in rheumatoid arthritis; and (3) SLE peripheral lymphocyte responsiveness to IL-2 is enhanced in vitro when cells are rested for several days prior to activation.
the IL-2 response defect in patients with systemic lupous erythematosus can be reversed by resting the lymphocytes prior to activation or by adding exogenous interleukin-21 to the culture.
